opus-5.5.text:
I think Triton has been one of the more successful attempts at this, and the reason is that it picked the right level of abstraction. It doesn't try to hide everything. You still think in terms of blocks, tiles, and how data moves between memory and compute, which is how you need to think to get good performance on a GPU. But it takes care of a lot of the painful low-level detail, like exactly how threads are laid out, shared memory swizzling, and some of the pipelining. For a lot of people that's the right trade-off. You can write a fused kernel in an afternoon that gets maybe 70 to 90 percent of what a hand-tuned CUDA kernel would get.

On portability across chips, it's a real plus. AMD has put a lot of effort into the Triton backend, and there's work on other accelerators too. A tile-based programming model maps reasonably well onto most of this hardware, because they all have some notion of a fast local memory, a slower global memory, and matrix-multiply units that want data in tiles. So the abstraction holds up better than you might expect.

That said, there are limits. Each new hardware generation adds features that don't fit neatly into the existing abstraction. On Hopper you had the Tensor Memory Accelerator, warp-specialized pipelines, and asynchronous wgmma instructions, and Blackwell adds more. Getting peak performance means exploiting those features directly, and a general compiler usually lags behind. That's why for something like FlashAttention we've often had to go lower, to CUTLASS and CuTe or even closer to the metal, to get the last 20 or 30 percent. Kernel writers want an abstraction that's easy to use, portable, and as fast as possible, and you usually can't have all three at once.

So my view is that Triton is excellent for research, for prototyping, and for the long tail of operations that don't justify months of hand-tuning. It's lowered the barrier for people to write custom kernels, and that's good for the field. For the handful of really performance-critical kernels, like attention and GEMMs, people will probably keep writing hardware-specific code for a while. What I find exciting is the newer wave of DSLs and abstractions trying to keep Triton's ease of use while exposing more of the hardware when you need it. I don't think we've found the final answer yet, but things are moving in a good direction.

r001.rationale: The response says peak performance requires low-level hardware-specific features and that Triton can leave the last 20–30% of performance untapped.

r002.rationale: It presents Triton’s 70–90% of hand-tuned CUDA performance as a worthwhile trade-off because kernels can be written quickly and the abstraction lowers the barrier to custom kernels.

fable-5.1.text:
Tri Dao: Yeah, I think Triton is a really important piece of the ecosystem, and I'd say it's probably the most successful attempt so far at giving people a programming model that sits above CUDA but still lets you get a good fraction of peak performance. The core idea, that you program at the level of tiles or blocks rather than individual threads, matches how the hardware actually wants to be used. Matrix multiply, attention, these are all fundamentally about moving tiles through the memory hierarchy, and Triton lets you express that without worrying about warp scheduling, shared memory bank conflicts, all the low-level stuff that eats up your time when you write raw CUDA.

On the cross-chip question specifically, I think it's genuinely one of the best bets we have, but I'd be careful about overstating how portable things are today. The abstraction is portable in the sense that the same Triton code will compile and run on NVIDIA and on AMD, and there's work on Intel and other backends. That's a big deal. If you're a researcher or a startup, writing something once and having it run on an MI300 and an H100 is really valuable. But performance portability is a different story. The kernels that get close to peak on one chip usually need to be tuned for the other, because the chips differ in things like the size of shared memory, how many registers you have, the shape of the matrix units, whether there's something like TMA for asynchronous data movement. Triton hides a lot of that, but it can't make those differences disappear, so you often end up with chip-specific tuning or even chip-specific code paths.

The other thing I'd say is that the gap between Triton and hand-written code depends a lot on the generation of hardware. On Ampere, Triton got very close to cuBLAS and to what we could do by hand. On Hopper and now Blackwell, the hardware got a lot more asynchronous and more specialized, with warp specialization, TMA, wgmma, these pipelined producer-consumer patterns. The compiler has to be a lot smarter to exploit that, and for a while the hand-written kernels were quite a bit ahead. The Triton team has been catching up, but that's the tension. Every time the hardware vendors add a new mechanism to squeeze out more performance, the abstraction has to grow to cover it, or you fall behind.

So my honest assessment is: for most people, most of the time, Triton is the right tool, and it's dramatically better than the alternative of everyone writing CUDA from scratch. For the handful of kernels that really matter, attention, GEMM, maybe some of the mixture-of-experts routing, you still probably want someone going lower level, and that's partly why we did things like FlashAttention 3 in a different style. And then there's this interesting question of whether we end up with something in between, like the work on CuTe DSL or ThunderKittens, that gives you a bit more control over the hardware while still being much more productive than raw CUDA. I don't think the final answer is settled yet, but Triton has set the bar for what a portable GPU programming layer should look like.

r001.rationale: It says Triton hides hardware-specific details and that this can leave tuned or hand-written kernels ahead, especially on newer chips.

r002.rationale: It praises Triton’s productivity and calls it the right tool for most people, but does not clearly say that a modest performance loss is acceptable in exchange for that gain.

astra-6.text:
I think Triton is a really useful level of abstraction. You’re working with blocks of data rather than explicitly managing what every individual thread does, and that makes writing GPU kernels much more accessible. You can express the computation fairly naturally and let the compiler handle a lot of the details.

The distinction I’d make is between portability and performance portability. Being able to compile the same code for different GPUs is valuable, but it doesn’t mean that code will run optimally on all of them. Different chips have different memory hierarchies, different compute capabilities, and different ways of moving data efficiently. You may still need to change the block sizes or how you organize the computation.

So I see Triton as a very good foundation. The interesting challenge is how much of that hardware-specific optimization the compiler can take care of, while still giving you enough control when you need to push performance further.

r001.rationale: The response says Triton code may not run optimally across chips and that tuning can be needed, but does not state that its abstraction costs performance by limiting low-level execution control.

r002.rationale: The response calls Triton accessible and useful, but does not say a modest performance loss is acceptable in exchange for a large productivity gain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Triton is a really good abstraction. You’re working with blocks of tensors rather than writing everything at the level of individual threads, and that makes it much easier to express an algorithm and let the compiler handle some of the mapping to the hardware.

But I would distinguish portability from performance portability. You might be able to run the same code on different GPUs, but getting really good performance can still require different block sizes, different amounts of parallelism, or a different algorithm. The chips have different memory hierarchies and different compute capabilities.

So I like the direction a lot. The question is how much the compiler can take care of while still giving you enough control to exploit the hardware when you need to.

r001.rationale: The response says Triton can require hardware-specific tuning and discusses retaining enough control, but it does not state that the abstraction costs performance by limiting low-level GPU execution control.

r002.rationale: It says Triton makes algorithms easier to express, but does not judge a modest performance loss acceptable in exchange for a large productivity gain.
